This decomposition resolves "problem cells" where rays might intersect a face twice in curvilinear grids [S4, book].

It further states that the solution to this issue is to subdivide these problem cells into tetrahedra (which have planar faces), thereby resolving the problem.

3. **Scalar Interpolation:** Scalar values $s$ at any point within a tetrahedron are interpolated linearly from the vertex values $s_i$ using barycentric coordinates or linear interpolation along edges [S1][S2].

The claim states that scalar values are interpolated linearly from vertex values using barycentric coordinates or linear interpolation along edges. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'We assume initially that the scalar field varies linearly across the cell... Then the color at the ray segment endpoints can be obtained by interpolation across polygons (for the rear endpoint at E) or edges (for the endpoints of G).' It further mentions that 'densities κ for the cloud particles can similarly be interpolated.' While the text does not explicitly use the term 'barycentric coordinates,' linear interpolation across a polyhedron (specifically a tetrahedron, which is mentioned in the context of topology calculation) is mathematically equivalent to interpolation using barycentric coordinates. The text confirms linear interpolation along edges and across polygons (which implies the use of coordinates within the polygon, effectively barycentric for triangles or similar for other polygons). Thus, the facts in the claim are supported by the evidence.

Cell projection is a direct volume rendering technique that treats volumetric data as a set of geometric primitives (convex polyhedral cells) which are projected onto the 2D image plane, rasterized, and composited in back-to-front order [S1][S4, book].

The claim accurately describes the Cell Projection technique as presented in the provided sources. Source [S1] explicitly states that cell projection 'renders the polygons in the projection of each cell' and 'requires a global visibility sort in order to composite the cells in back to front order.' It also describes dividing the projection of convex polyhedral cells into polygons on the image plane. Source [S4] corroborates this, stating that the technique 'works directly on curvilinear or irregular grids by projecting cells onto the image plane,' that 'projections of the edges of a single cell divide the image plane into polygons,' and that these are 'scan converted and composited by standard graphics hardware in back-to-front sorted order.' The claim's description of treating volumetric data as geometric primitives (convex polyhedral cells) projected, rasterized, and composited back-to-front is fully supported by the text.
